summary: Provides guidelines for the operation of the DNS root name servers. It is a Best Current Practice and was replaced by RFC 7720.

eli5.summary: The root servers are the top of the Internet's address book. This lists the rules the people who run them are expected to follow.

questions: how are dns root servers operated
subtitle: The operating rules the DNS root name servers were expected to follow in 2000: capacity, security and coordination.

tldr.problem: The DNS root name servers are critical to the Internet, but they were run by volunteers with no formal, written guidelines explaining how and why they are operated.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets requirements for the servers themselves (capacity, authoritative-only service, open access), for physical and network security, for DNSSEC and zone updates, and for coordination between operators.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 40) that obsoletes RFC 2010 and was itself replaced by RFC 7720.

facts.label: Capacity
facts.value: 3 times the measured peak on the most loaded server

facts.label: Staff availability
facts.value: 24 hours a day, 7 days a week

today: RFC 2870 was obsoleted by RFC 7720, so it is no longer the current statement of root name server requirements. It is BCP 40 and itself replaced RFC 2010.

sections.title: Background and Purpose
sections.content:
The RFC says that resolving domain names depends on the proper, safe and secure operation of the root name servers. At the time, these dozen or so servers were provided by a group of trusted volunteers. The document does not propose to change that. It only writes down formal guidelines so the community understands how and why the servers are run.

It notes that ICANN had become responsible for the root servers and had appointed the Root Server System Advisory Committee (RSSAC) to advise its board. ICANN and RSSAC look to the IETF for engineering standards. The root servers serve the root zone, written ., and they are neither involved with nor dependent on 'whois' data.

The authors express confidence that losing most of the root servers, presumably temporarily, should not significantly affect operation of the Internet. They also say that incorrect data in the root zone or TLDs is a serious danger, so authentication, validation and security of that data matter a great deal.
sections.eli5: A few trusted volunteers keep the top of the Internet's address book running. This note writes down the rules so everyone knows how it works.

sections.title: Requirements for the Servers
sections.content:
The RFC deliberately does not name hardware, operating systems or name-server software, since variety adds overall robustness. Each server MUST run software that correctly implements the DNS standards, at that time RFC 1035 and RFC 2181.

Capacity is the main numeric rule. Each server MUST be able to handle three times the measured peak load seen on the most loaded server under normal conditions. This is meant to keep the service working if two thirds of the servers go out of operation, whether by intent, accident or malice. Connectivity SHOULD be as diverse as possible.

Servers MUST give authoritative answers only for the zones they serve. They MUST disable recursion, forwarding and anything else that could produce cached answers, and MUST NOT act as secondary for zones other than the root and root-servers.net. They MUST answer queries from any Internet host, with blocking allowed only for queries that cause operational problems, and only for as long as the problem lasts. Root servers SHOULD NOT answer zone transfer (AXFR) queries from anyone but other root servers. For UDP, servers MUST generate checksums and MUST verify any non-zero checksum they receive.
sections.eli5: Each server must be strong enough that even if most of the others break, the rest can still answer everyone. They only give answers they are sure of, and they answer anybody who asks.

sections.title: Physical and Network Security
sections.content:
The RFC asks for the level of protection expected of data centers critical to a major enterprise. For physical security, the area holding a server MUST have positive access control, meaning the people allowed in are limited, controlled and recorded. Power continuity for at least 48 hours MUST be assured unless the local grid is documented to be more reliable than a UPS. Fire detection or retardation MUST be provided, and there MUST be a way to return to operation rapidly after an outage.

For network security, root servers MUST NOT provide services other than root name service, so no http, telnet, rlogin or ftp. Only server administrators may have login accounts, and remote access MUST be strongly authenticated and encrypted. The LAN segment MUST NOT also host crackable hosts and SHOULD be firewalled so that only name service ports are reachable. Servers SHOULD synchronize clocks as NTP clients but MUST NOT act as NTP peers or servers, and MUST NOT rely on address-based or name-based authentication. Intrusion attempts SHOULD be logged, logs SHOULD be analyzed by a cooperative security team, and servers SHOULD log in GMT to ease comparison.
sections.eli5: The servers live in locked rooms with backup power, and they do only one job. Nobody can wander in, either in person or over the network.

sections.title: Protecting the Root Zone Data
sections.content:
The root zone MUST be signed by IANA in accordance with DNSSEC (RFC 2535 or its replacements), and root servers MUST be DNSSEC-capable. The RFC admits that DNSSEC was not yet deployable on some common platforms, and says it will be deployed when supported. Transfers of the root zone between root servers MUST be authenticated, and servers MUST use DNSSEC to authenticate root zones received from other servers. A 'hidden primary' that only authorized secondaries can reach MAY be used.

Updates to the root zone SHOULD pass a number of heuristic checks that look for erroneous updates, and failing updates MUST get human intervention. Updates SHOULD normally take effect within 6 hours of notification of the operator. A special emergency procedure SHOULD be defined, with updates made no later than 12 hours after notification. Each server MUST also have a way to update root zone data over a non-network path in case of critical network failure, and each root MUST keep daily global statistics on queries, made available to RSSAC and its sponsored researchers.
sections.eli5: Before a change to the top address book is accepted, it gets checked, and a person looks at anything odd. If the network breaks, there is still a way to deliver the update by other means.

sections.title: Communication Between Operators
sections.content:
Operators need to coordinate with each other and with IANA and ICANN. Planned outages SHOULD be coordinated so that many servers are not down at once, and backups SHOULD be timed the same way and frequently transferred off site. Operators SHOULD exchange log files, especially those about security and loading, either through a central point or informally. Usage statistics SHOULD be exchanged between operators and MUST be reported to IANA for planning and reporting.

Administrative personnel MUST be available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, though on-call staff MAY cover hours outside normal working time.
sections.eli5: The people running the servers talk to each other, so they do not all switch off at the same time, and someone is always awake to help.
